lead: Fort Worth homes face hail, Trinity River flooding and shifting clay soil. DryFlare helps owners from the Cultural District to Alliance get water out and dry out.
risk: hail storms, flash flooding and foundation-related leaks
why: The Trinity River runs through the heart of Fort Worth. After the 1949 flood swamped downtown and the West Side, levees were built along the river, and the Panther Island project continues that flood work today. Smaller creeks still flash flood in heavy rain, and low streets in older neighborhoods fill fast.

Like Dallas, Fort Worth sits under the North Texas hail track. Storms damage roofs from Tanglewood to Alliance, and leaks follow. Expansive clay soils shift with the seasons, cracking slabs and stressing water lines underneath. The 2021 freeze burst pipes in homes built for mild winters.
image_alt: Storm-damaged roof and broken window after a North Texas hailstorm
image_caption: Hail damage on Fort Worth roofs often turns into ceiling leaks with the next rain.
problems: West Side, Alliance and north Fort Worth
Homes after hail and heavy rain
tips: Inspect your roof after hail season each spring.
Keep gutters clear and downspouts pointed away from the slab.
Watch for cracks in drywall or sticking doors; they can signal foundation movement and pipe stress.
Know your main water shut-off before winter.
areas: Calls come from Downtown, Near Southside, the Cultural District, TCU, Tanglewood, Ridglea and Alliance, plus Arlington, Keller, Hurst, North Richland Hills and Benbrook.

faq.q: Why do slab leaks happen in Fort Worth?
faq.a: Clay soil around much of Fort Worth swells when wet and shrinks in drought. The movement can crack slabs and the water lines inside or below them. Signs include warm spots on floors, a rising water bill and damp flooring with no clear cause.
